lessons.title: What a Stock Really Is
lessons.subtitle: A slice of a real business — not a lottery ticket

chapters.heading: Ownership, Not a Bet
chapters.body:
A share is partial ownership of a real company — its factories, its cash, its debts, its future. When you buy a share of a halal-screened company, you own a piece of that business, like a partner. That is why the Prophet ﷺ said: 'The two parties of a transaction have the choice as long as they have not parted; if they were truthful and clear, their transaction is blessed' (Bukhari 2079). The blessing is in the truth of the exchange — a real thing, really owned, really priced.

Contrast this with what most people call 'playing the market': buying a ticker because the line on the chart is green. A Muslim buys a business because the business is good — the chart is only the weather; the company is the house.

Contemporary authority: Mufti Taqi Usmani — chairman of AAOIFI's Sharia Supervisory Board and the most cited living scholar of Islamic finance (An Introduction to Islamic Finance) — grounds share-ownership-as-partnership as the standard view today.

lessons.familyQuestion: Name one company your family buys from every week — that is a business you could one day part-own. What makes it good or bad?

lessons.title: Reading a Company — the Facts
lessons.subtitle: Revenue, debt, cash flow: the three questions

chapters.heading: The Business, the Burden, the Breath
chapters.body:
Before any screen, ask three factual questions. ONE — the business: what does the company actually sell, and to whom? Read its annual report's first ten pages; the honest ones tell you plainly. TWO — the burden: how much debt does it carry? Debt is the company's leash — the more it owes, the less it is its own master. THREE — the breath: does cash actually flow in? Profit on paper is an opinion; cash in the account is a fact. Learn these three and you already see more than most traders.

All of this is public — every listed company files its numbers by law. The skill is not secret knowledge; it is patient reading. Wasia's rule applies here too: one page at a time.

Contemporary authority: Sheikh Joe Bradford (PhD, US-based Islamic finance scholar) teaches company analysis through the same three questions in his investment courses — the method is classical, the language is today's.

lessons.familyQuestion: Pick a company. Can you find what it sells and how much it owes, in ten minutes of searching? Try it together.

lessons.title: The Three Halal Screens
lessons.subtitle: The 5% / 30% / 5% thresholds that decide everything

chapters.heading: The Industry, the Debt, the Interest
chapters.body:
The screens scholars use (AAOIFI-style, applied by the halal screeners worldwide):

1. BUSINESS ACTIVITY — revenue from alcohol, gambling, riba-based lending, pork, weapons of offense, adult content, and non-compliant entertainment must be under 5% of total revenue. If a hotel chain earns 4% from its bar, the scholars tolerate the share with purification (you give away that 4% of your dividends).

2. DEBT — conventional debt should be under about 30% of market capitalization (some schools measure against total assets at 33⅓% — follow your school, the app's calculator accepts either).

3. INTEREST INCOME — earning interest must be under 5% of revenue, and that portion is likewise purified.

A company failing any screen is not purified — it is avoided. The line between a tolerated margin and a forbidden core is the line this module exists to teach.

Contemporary authority: these are the exact thresholds AAOIFI's Sharia Supervisory Board — chaired by Mufti Taqi Usmani — publishes; every major screener (Zoya, Musaffa) applies them as stated here.

lessons.familyQuestion: Why do you think scholars set 5% for the tolerated margin and not 0% — and why not 50%? Where would you draw the line, and why?

lessons.title: Purification — Cleaning the Dividend
lessons.subtitle: The math that keeps lawful income lawful

chapters.heading: Give Away the Haram Slice
chapters.body:
When a company earns a small tolerated haram portion, your share of that portion is not yours — it must be given away, to the poor, without expecting reward. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Allah is pure and accepts only what is pure' (Muslim 1015).

The math: PURIFICATION = your dividend x the company's haram revenue %. If a company earns 3% from interest and pays you $100 in dividends, $3 goes to sadaqah; $97 is your halal income. The app's purification calculator does this exactly — it is not a decoration, it is the difference between a blessed portfolio and a doubtful one.

And zakat on shares held for investment: 2.5% of market value each lunar year — the Tayyib module's zakat engine computes it with your other wealth.

Contemporary authority: Mufti Muhammad ibn Adam (Darul Iftaa, UK) details the purification calculation in his financial fatwa collection — the formula this lesson teaches is his, in today's English.

lessons.familyQuestion: A company you own pays $200 dividends and 4% of its revenue is non-compliant. How much do you give away? Work it together.

lessons.title: Reading the Market — Risks and Rewards
lessons.subtitle: What rises, what falls — taught as honest uncertainty

chapters.heading: Nobody Knows; Everybody Can Learn
chapters.body:
Here is the fact no app may hide: NO ONE knows what a stock will do tomorrow — not analysts, not apps, not this one. What can be taught is how to weigh likelihoods:

Prices move on earnings (did the company make what it promised?), on the industry (is the whole sector rising or falling?), on interest rates (when rates rise, borrowed money costs more and growth stocks often fall), and on fear and greed (the market is a crowd; crowds panic and overjoy together).

The Muslim investor's edges are character, not clairvoyance: PATIENCE (hold good businesses through weather), DIVERSIFICATION (never one company — the Prophet ﷺ said do not put all your eggs in one fragile vessel, paraphrasing the hadith of reliance), and CASH RESERVES (the man who keeps some dry powder buys when others must sell).

Rising: companies with growing honest revenue, low debt, real products. Falling: heavily indebted companies when credit tightens; companies whose story outran their numbers. Learn the pattern, never the promise.

Contemporary authority: Mufti Taqi Usmani is explicit that honest uncertainty about the future is not gambling — qimar is wagering on chance, while informed ownership of real assets is trade, even when prices move.

lessons.familyQuestion: Think of something your family buys more of every year. Is the company behind it growing — and how would you check?

lessons.title: Ethics Screen — The Boycott of the Soul
lessons.subtitle: Who the company serves — and who it harms

chapters.heading: A Share Is a Vote
chapters.body:
Ownership is support. A Muslim's portfolio is a quiet vote cast every day: in favor of what the company does, financed by what the company earns. That is why the screens begin with the business itself — and why this module adds the ethic your conscience already knows.

Scholarly consensus is firm on the core: no alcohol, no gambling, no riba-lending, no pork, no adult content, no weapons of offense, no unjust harm. On current conflicts and country-specific lists, scholars differ in detail and the lists change — the honest tool gives you the CONSCIENCE SCREEN alongside the financial one: a place to exclude what your heart cannot carry, by sector or by name, so your portfolio never pays for what your duas oppose.

Zakat due on what you hold is computed in the Tayyib engine — wealth purifies wealth.

Contemporary authority: AAOIFI's current standards define the weapon screen as weapons of offense — and contemporary scholars note the lists for active conflicts evolve; the conscience screen exists precisely because a static list cannot carry a living heart.

lessons.familyQuestion: If you could never buy one company's shares because of what it does, which would it be — and what would you do with the money instead?

lessons.title: Crypto — Asset or Gamble?
lessons.subtitle: The ruling turns on HOW you hold it, not what it is

chapters.heading: The Line Is the Leverage
chapters.body:
Digital assets (like Bitcoin) are treated by a growing body of scholars as tradeable assets — you may buy with money you own, hold them, or sell them; some even permit the tolerant view that they function as currency-like property.

But the same scholars draw a bright line around HOW: LEVERAGE and FUTURES — borrowing to multiply a position, or contracts that bet on tomorrow's price — transform an asset into gambling on a number you do not own, and riba rides the borrowed half. Short-selling is likewise out — you cannot sell what you do not possess. And coins whose whole purpose is gambling, interest-lending, or fraud are out entirely, whatever the chart says.

The rule of thumb this module teaches: OWN IT OR LEAVE IT. If you cannot hold it with your own money and walk away, you are not investing — you are wagering, and the sharia has a shorter word for wagering.

Contemporary authority: Mufti Faraz Adam (AAOIFI-certified) researched digital assets directly and published the leading framework: lawful as property when owned outright; unlawful the moment leverage, futures, or riba enter — the exact line this lesson draws.

lessons.familyQuestion: What is the difference between buying something and betting on its price? Can you explain it to a younger sibling?

lessons.title: Day Trading — the Scholars' Difference
lessons.subtitle: Same-day buying and selling: where the opinions stand

chapters.heading: Two Honest Views, One Bright Line
chapters.body:
Here the scholars genuinely differ, and this module teaches the difference rather than pretending there is none:

VIEW ONE (the majority of contemporary halal screeners): buying a screened stock in the morning and selling it by afternoon is permissible IF the shares are fully paid with your own money (no margin) and truly settle to your ownership (the T+1/T+2 settlement delay means some add a precautionary wait). The short holding period does not, by itself, break the contract.

VIEW TWO (the more precautionary scholars): rapid in-and-out trading resembles qimar — gambling on price movements — especially when it becomes the primary motive, divorced from any view of the business.

WHAT BOTH SIDES AGREE ON: no short-selling (selling what you do not own), no margin or leverage (riba and ownership-breach), no futures or options as they are structured conventionally, and no trading in unscreened companies. When you choose, choose with knowledge of both views — and the safest road is marked: own cash, screened companies, and holding periods measured in weeks, not seconds.

Contemporary authority: Sheikh Joe Bradford's 2025 analysis of day trading lays out both views (permitted with owned cash / precautionary abstention) — this module follows his conclusion: teach the difference, mark the safest road.

lessons.familyQuestion: Why do you think the scholars who worry about day trading compare it to gambling — what feeling does rapid trading create in the heart?

lessons.title: The Halal Trader's Craft
lessons.subtitle: How to actually do it — the mechanics, halal-clean

chapters.heading: The Toolbox and the Temperament
chapters.body:
Mechanics, step by step: (1) a brokerage account funded with your own cash — never margin; (2) the screen applied BEFORE the buy, not after; (3) the buy — a market or limit order on a screened company; (4) the hold — weeks to years, while the business grows; (5) the sell — when the company's facts change, not when the crowd panics; (6) the purification — the calculator's number, given away each dividend; (7) the zakat — 2.5% yearly, computed with your other wealth.

Temperament, the Muslim edge: the Prophet ﷺ loved those 'who worked with excellence even if the work was small' — the trader's excellence is patience and record-keeping. Write down WHY you bought, WHAT would change your mind, and WHEN you will review. The written reason is your protection against the crowd's fear and greed — the two diseases every market spreads.

Contemporary authority: the mechanics here follow the practical guidance of IslamicFinanceGuru's scholars (AAOIFI-certified) for retail halal investing in 2026 — real brokerages, real settlement rules, no leverage.

lessons.familyQuestion: If your family bought one screened share and watched it for a year, what would you learn that a week could never teach you?
